{"id": "3287cf90-32ce-4e3d-9255-cf572c484941", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_OBeFjNGYBbIgRKl7owqU5b", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"SageMaker HyperPod multi-head node support\",\"context\":\"# SageMaker HyperPod multi-head node support\\n\\nYou can create multiple controller (head) nodes in a single SageMaker HyperPod Slurm\\ncluster, with one serving as the primary controller node and the others serving as\\nbackup controller nodes. The primary controller node is responsible for controlling the\\ncompute (worker) nodes and handling Slurm operations. The backup controller nodes\\nconstantly monitor the primary controller node. If the primary controller node fails or\\nbecomes unresponsive, one of the backup controller nodes will automatically take over as\\nthe new primary controller node.\\n\\nConfiguring multiple controller nodes in SageMaker HyperPod Slurm clusters provides several\\nkey benefits. It eliminates the risk of single controller node failure by providing\\ncontroller head nodes, enables automatic failover to backup controller nodes with faster\\nrecovery, and allows you to manage your own accounting databases and Slurm configuration\\nindependently\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-multihead-slurm.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Announcing the new cluster creation experience for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod | Artificial Intelligence\",\"context\":\"## Add an instance group\\n\\nFor both quick and custom setup options, you can add a new instance group to your SageMaker HyperPod cluster from the SageMaker AI console.\\n\\nYou can choose between standard instance groups, which provide a general-purpose computing environment without additional security restrictions, or restricted instance groups (RIGs) to provision a specialized environment within SageMaker HyperPod that provides an isolated space for training customized Amazon Nova models.\\n\\nYou can select on-demand capacity for one-time workloads and testing, or flexible training plans capacity to get predictable access to accelerated compute resources within your timeline and budget, for your planned, large-scale training jobs. With flexible training plans, you can schedule capacity on the latest P6-B200 instance types and P6e-GB200 UltraServers powered by NVIDIA Blackwell tensor core GPUs. If you need to provision an instance group for long-term usage, you can contact AWS to reserve capacity for a longer duration.\\n\\nWith Amazon EKS orchestration, for each instance group that you add, you can enable stress and connectivity deep health checks. These deep health checks are performed in addition to the orchestrator-agnostic basic health checks that also apply to Slurm orchestrated clusters. Stress checks test hardware components under stress to identify potential issues with GPUs, memory, and other hardware components. Connectivity checks test network connectivity between nodes to maintain proper communication for distributed training.\\n\\nWith advanced configuration, you can choose the number of threads that run on each CPU core of your Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances. Choosing one thread per core disables multi-threading. Each core runs a single thread, which can provide more predictable performance for applications that benefit from dedicated core resources, such as certain high-performance computing workloads. Choosing two threads per core enables multi-threading. Each physical core runs two threads simultaneously, potentially increasing throughput for multi-threaded applications at the cost of some per-thread performance\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/announcing-the-new-cluster-creation-experience-for-amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"SageMaker HyperPod references\",\"context\":\"#### SlurmConfig (per instance group)\\n\\nAdd `SlurmConfig` to each instance group to define the Slurm node type and partition assignment.\\n\\n```\\n\\\"SlurmConfig\\\": {\\n \\\"NodeType\\\": \\\"Controller | Login | Compute\\\",\\n \\\"PartitionNames\\\": [\\\"string\\\"]\\n}\\n```\\n\\n**Parameters:**\\n\\n* `NodeType` \u2013 Required. The Slurm node type for this instance group. Valid values:\\n\\n + `Controller` \u2013 Slurm controller (head) node. Runs the `slurmctld` daemon. Exactly one instance group must have this node type.\\n + `Login` \u2013 Login node for user access. Optional. At most one instance group can have this node type.\\n + `Compute` \u2013 Worker nodes that execute jobs. Can have multiple instance groups with this node type.\\n\\n **Important:**\\n\\n `NodeType` is immutable. Once set during cluster creation, it cannot be changed. To use a different node type, create a new instance group.\\n* `PartitionNames` \u2013 Conditional. An array of Slurm partition names. Required for `Compute` node types; not allowed for `Controller` or `Login` node types. Currently supports a single partition name per instance group.\\n\\n **Note:**\\n\\n All nodes are automatically added to the universal `dev` partition in addition to their specified partition.\\n\\n**Example:**\\n\\n```\\n{\\n \\\"InstanceGroupName\\\": \\\"gpu-compute\\\",\\n \\\"InstanceType\\\": \\\"ml.p4d.24xlarge\\\",\\n \\\"InstanceCount\\\": 8,\\n \\\"SlurmConfig\\\": {\\n \\\"NodeType\\\": \\\"Compute\\\",\\n \\\"PartitionNames\\\": [\\\"gpu-training\\\"]\\n },\\n \\\"LifeCycleConfig\\\": {\\n \\\"SourceS3Uri\\\": \\\"s3://sagemaker-bucket/lifecycle/src/\\\",\\n \\\"OnCreate\\\": \\\"on_create.sh\\\"\\n },\\n \\\"ExecutionRole\\\": \\\"arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/HyperPodRole\\\"\\n}\\n```\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-ref.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify HyperPod controller node HA best practices in AWS docs", "parent_id": "544ffc51-5acb-4ec9-a602-3284d4fb0791"}

No mutating/error CloudTrail events found — clean recent history. I now have enough to compile the readiness assessment.

## HyperPod Cluster Readiness Assessment: `skilltest-hp-slurm` (us-west-2)

**Overall: READY WITH CAVEATS** — core infrastructure is healthy, but there are real risks for an unattended 4-day run.

### ✅ Healthy signals
| Check | Status |
|---|---|
| Cluster status | `InService` ✓ |
| Instance groups | All 3 groups `InService`, CurrentCount = TargetCount (no scaling drift) |
| Node health | All 3 nodes `Running`, no error messages |
| Image/software version | `UpToDate` on all nodes (no pending patches) |
| Node recovery | `Automatic` (HyperPod will auto-replace unhealthy GPU nodes) |
| FSx Lustre filesystem | `AVAILABLE`, 1200 GiB SCRATCH_2, mounted on all compute nodes at `/fsx` |
| Recent CloudTrail activity | No mutating/error events (Create/Update/Delete/BatchDeleteClusterNodes) in the past 48h — no recent changes or failures |

### ⚠️ Risks to address before committing to 4 days unattended

1. **Single controller node (SPOF)** — The `controller` instance group has `CurrentCount: 1`, no backup/multi-head configuration. AWS explicitly supports multi-head controller nodes for Slurm HyperPod clusters specifically to eliminate this risk. If the single controller fails mid-run, Slurm scheduling halts for the whole cluster with no automatic failover. **Recommend**: add a backup controller node, or at minimum have alerting/on-call coverage for controller health during the run.

2. **Minimal/no compute capacity for fault tolerance** — Only 2 compute nodes total (1× `ml.g5.xlarge`, 1× `ml.g5.2xlarge`), each in its own single-node instance group. There's no spare/standby capacity — if either GPU node is marked unhealthy or reclaimed, the training job on that partition loses capacity with no redundant node to fail over to within the group.

3. **FSx filesystem is externally owned by a different stack** — The mounted FSx Lustre filesystem (`fs-0e93a90dc05f50e97`) is tagged as belonging to a **separate ParallelCluster stack** (`distributed-training-triage`, CloudFormation stack `distributed-training-triage`), not to the HyperPod cluster itself. This is a shared/cross-stack dependency — if someone deletes or modifies that ParallelCluster stack (e.g., as cleanup), your HyperPod cluster's storage disappears mid-run.

4. **Related alarm (different but connected resource)**: `distributed-training-triage-b200-HeadNode-ClustermgtdHeartbeat` has been in **ALARM** state since 2026-08-31 (stale heartbeat, ~1 month old) for a ParallelCluster head node (`i-01bbde10b04dd4ca8`) under the same account/owner tags as the shared FSx filesystem. While this alarm targets a different compute cluster, it indicates that stack may be degraded or abandoned — worth confirming it isn't going to be torn down (taking the FSx filesystem with it) during your training window.

### Suggested fixes before go/no-go tomorrow
- Verify who owns/manages the `distributed-training-triage` ParallelCluster stack and confirm no planned teardown/maintenance on it or its FSx filesystem during Oct 2–6.
- Investigate/silence or resolve the month-old stale `ClustermgtdHeartbeat` alarm on that related stack to rule out it being an early warning sign.
- Consider adding a backup Slurm controller node given the 4-day unattended duration.
- Set up a CloudWatch alarm on HyperPod node health / FSx throughput specifically for this cluster if not already present (none was found scoped to `skilltest-hp-slurm` itself).

**To go deeper**, I could: check Slurm scheduler logs/sinfo via the controller for queue backlog, pull FSx throughput/IOPS metrics over the last 48h to confirm no storage pressure, or search CloudTrail further back (>48h) around the FSx stack's creation/ownership history."}]}], "label": "Check SageMaker HyperPod cluster skilltest-hp-slurm health in us-west-2"}
